questions.stem: Where in the atmosphere is most of Earth's ozone found?
options: In the thermosphere, at the outer edge of the atmosphere
Spread evenly through every layer of the atmosphere
In the stratosphere, above the level of most weather
In the troposphere, close to the ground where we breathe
questions.explanation: About 90% of atmospheric ozone is in the stratosphere, forming the ozone layer. Ozone near the ground is a pollutant in smog, and it is a small part of the total. The thermosphere has very little gas of any kind.

questions.stem: How does stratospheric ozone affect the solar energy reaching Earth's surface?
options: It absorbs most of the infrared emitted by the surface
It scatters radio waves so they cannot reach the ground
It absorbs much of the incoming ultraviolet radiation
It reflects most of the incoming visible light to space
questions.explanation: Ozone molecules absorb ultraviolet radiation, so less UV reaches the surface. Visible light passes through ozone largely unaffected. Absorbing outgoing infrared is the role of greenhouse gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Of the three bands of solar ultraviolet radiation, UV-A, UV-B and UV-C, which reaches the surface in the greatest amount?
options: All three in equal amounts, as ozone absorbs only infrared
UV-A, the longest wavelengths, which ozone absorbs least
UV-C, the shortest wavelengths, which ozone absorbs least
UV-B, because ozone absorbs it more weakly than UV-A
questions.explanation: Ozone and oxygen absorb UV-C completely and most UV-B, but let most UV-A through. So nearly all the UV reaching the ground is UV-A, with a small, harmful share of UV-B. The shorter the wavelength, the more strongly it is absorbed.

questions.stem: When ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation in the stratosphere, what happens to the energy?
options: It is transformed into thermal energy, warming the stratosphere
It is destroyed, so less energy exists in the Earth system
It is passed down to warm the ground directly beneath
It is stored in the ozone, which then becomes oxygen gas forever
questions.explanation: Energy is neither created nor destroyed. The absorbed UV energy becomes thermal energy, which is why temperature rises with height through the stratosphere. The energy is transformed, not lost, and it is not carried straight down to the ground.

questions.stem: Satellite data show stratospheric ozone over a region falling by 10% during spring. Which change at the surface would scientists expect?
options: Less infrared escapes to space, so surface temperatures rise sharply
Less UV-A reaches the surface, so plants photosynthesise more slowly
More UV-B reaches the surface, raising sunburn and skin damage risk
More visible light reaches the surface, making days much brighter
questions.explanation: Thinner ozone absorbs less ultraviolet, especially UV-B, so more of it reaches the ground, with harmful effects on skin, eyes and organisms. Ozone has little effect on visible light, and its role in trapping infrared is minor compared with water vapour and carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: A surface with a high albedo:
options: Emits a large share of infrared radiation to space
Lets a large share of sunlight pass straight through it
Reflects a large share of the sunlight falling on it
Absorbs a large share of the sunlight falling on it
questions.explanation: Albedo is the fraction of incoming solar radiation a surface reflects. A high albedo, such as fresh snow, means most sunlight is reflected and little is absorbed. A low albedo, such as open ocean or dark forest, means most sunlight is absorbed.

questions.stem: Which list arranges these surfaces from highest to lowest albedo?
options: Fresh snow, desert sand, forest, open ocean
Open ocean, forest, desert sand, fresh snow
Desert sand, fresh snow, open ocean, forest
Forest, fresh snow, open ocean, desert sand
questions.explanation: Fresh snow reflects most sunlight. Pale desert sand reflects a moderate share, dark forest canopies absorb most light, and open ocean, seen from above at moderate sun angles, reflects the least of these. Darker surfaces absorb more energy and warm more.

questions.stem: Earth's average albedo is about 0.3. What does this mean for the solar energy reaching Earth?
options: About 30% reaches the surface and 70% is absorbed by ozone
About 30% is turned into infrared and 70% stays as light
About 30% is reflected to space and about 70% is absorbed
About 30% is absorbed and about 70% is reflected to space
questions.explanation: An albedo of 0.3 means 30% of incoming sunlight is reflected by clouds, aerosols, air and the surface. The remaining 70% is absorbed by the atmosphere and surface, and that absorbed energy drives Earth's processes. Reversing the two figures is a common slip.

questions.stem: Over a decade, bushland on a plain is cleared and replaced by dark bitumen and roofs. Assuming the same sunshine, how will the net solar energy absorbed by the area change?
options: It stays the same, because albedo depends only on cloud cover
It rises, because buildings produce extra solar energy of their own
It rises if the new surfaces have a lower albedo than the bushland
It falls, because built surfaces always reflect more than plants
questions.explanation: The energy absorbed is the incoming energy multiplied by (1 − albedo). Dark bitumen and roofs have low albedos, so they absorb more of the same sunshine than the bush did. Pale roofs would have the opposite effect, so built surfaces do not always reflect more.

questions.stem: A patch of ground receives 800 W m⁻² of sunlight. Its albedo is 0.25. How much power does each square metre absorb?
questions.explanation: The absorbed share is 1 − 0.25 = 0.75, so 0.75 × 800 = 600 W per square metre. 200 W is the reflected part. Energy is conserved: absorbed plus reflected equals the 800 W arriving.

questions.stem: In what form does Earth's surface mainly emit energy back towards space?
options: Visible light
Ultraviolet radiation
Microwave radiation
Thermal infrared radiation
questions.explanation: Earth's surface is far cooler than the Sun, so it emits mostly long-wavelength infrared radiation. The Sun, much hotter, emits mainly visible light and near infrared. Ultraviolet comes from very hot sources such as the Sun.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the greenhouse effect?
options: Greenhouse gases thin the ozone layer, letting more heat reach the ground
Greenhouse gases reflect visible light from clouds back to the surface
Greenhouse gases return some outgoing infrared to the surface, adding warmth
Greenhouse gases block incoming sunlight, so the surface stays cooler
questions.explanation: Most infrared from the surface passes out to space, but greenhouse gases absorb some of it and re-radiate part back towards the surface. That extra energy warms the surface beyond what sunlight alone would. Greenhouse gases let most incoming sunlight through.

questions.stem: Which pair of atmospheric gases both contribute to the natural greenhouse effect?
options: Argon and nitrogen
Oxygen and argon
Water vapour and carbon dioxide
Nitrogen and oxygen
questions.explanation: Water vapour and carbon dioxide absorb infrared strongly, as do methane and nitrous oxide. Nitrogen, oxygen and argon make up more than 99% of dry air but absorb very little infrared, so they do not contribute significantly.

questions.stem: On a cloudless night in Canberra the ground cools quickly. Which statement best explains why humid nights cool less than dry ones?
options: Humid air has a lower albedo, so it absorbs more sunlight at night
Water vapour absorbs and re-radiates outgoing infrared back to the ground
Water vapour reflects moonlight back down, warming the ground at night
Dry air conducts heat away from the ground faster than humid air
questions.explanation: Water vapour is a strong greenhouse gas. On humid nights it absorbs infrared from the ground and re-radiates some back, slowing the cooling. In dry air more infrared escapes straight to space. There is no sunlight at night for albedo to act on.

questions.stem: Without the greenhouse effect, how would Earth's average surface temperature differ?
options: It would be well below freezing instead of about 15 °C
It would be about the same, as the Sun alone sets it
It would be much hotter, as heat would build up at the surface
It would swing between −100 °C and 100 °C each day
questions.explanation: Estimates put Earth's average temperature without a greenhouse effect at around −18 °C, compared with about 15 °C today. The natural greenhouse effect keeps most surface water liquid. It slows energy loss, so removing it would cool the surface, not warm it.

questions.stem: What is the dominant way that thermal energy is transferred around Earth's surface, from the tropics towards the poles?
options: Flow of heat outward from the mantle to the surface
Systematic circulation of air masses in the atmosphere
Conduction of heat through the rocks of the crust
Radiation of infrared directly from the equator to the poles
questions.explanation: Warm air rising in the tropics and moving poleward, and cool air returning, carries most of the heat transferred around the surface. Conduction through rock is very slow, and heat from Earth's interior is tiny compared with solar heating.

questions.stem: Why does the equator receive more solar energy per square metre than the poles?
options: It is closer to the Sun than the poles are, by thousands of kilometres
Its thicker atmosphere absorbs more sunlight than the poles' atmosphere
It has a higher albedo, so it reflects less of the incoming sunlight
Sunlight strikes it more directly, so the energy is spread over less area
questions.explanation: Near the equator the Sun's rays arrive close to vertical, concentrating the energy on a small area. At high latitudes the same beam is spread over a larger, slanted area and passes through more atmosphere. The difference in distance from the Sun is negligible.

questions.stem: Air rises near the equator and sinks at about 30° latitude. What surface pressure and weather does the sinking air produce?
options: High pressure with dry, mostly clear conditions
Low pressure with heavy, frequent rainfall
Low pressure with strong thunderstorms each afternoon
High pressure with persistent cloud and drizzle
questions.explanation: Sinking air warms as it is compressed, so clouds evaporate and rain is rare. This subtropical high-pressure belt explains many of the world's deserts, including much of inland Australia. Rising air near the equator gives low pressure and heavy rain.

questions.stem: In the three-cell model of atmospheric circulation, which cell lies between about 30° and 60° latitude?
options: The polar cell
The Walker cell
The Ferrel cell
The Hadley cell
questions.explanation: The Hadley cell spans from the equator to about 30°, the Ferrel cell from about 30° to 60°, and the polar cell from about 60° to the pole, in each hemisphere. The Walker circulation is an east-west loop over the tropical Pacific, not one of the three latitude cells.

questions.stem: Surface air flowing from the subtropical high towards the equator in the Southern Hemisphere is deflected by Earth's rotation. What winds result?
options: Polar easterlies
South-east trade winds
North-east trade winds
Westerly winds
questions.explanation: Air moving north towards the equator is deflected to its left by the Coriolis effect in the Southern Hemisphere, so it blows from the south-east. North-east trades are the Northern Hemisphere equivalent. Westerlies blow on the poleward side of the subtropical high.

questions.stem: Southern Australian cities such as Perth and Adelaide get most of their rain in winter, from cold fronts in the westerly winds. Which explains this pattern?
options: The ocean conveyor reverses direction every winter, cooling the coast
The ozone layer thins in winter, letting more cold air reach the ground
Earth's revolution with its tilted axis shifts the pressure belts north in winter
Earth's rotation speeds up in winter, strengthening the westerly winds
questions.explanation: As Earth revolves around the Sun with its axis tilted, the zone of strongest heating moves north and south through the year. In the southern winter the pressure belts shift north, bringing the westerlies and their fronts over southern Australia. In summer the subtropical high sits over these cities, keeping them dry.

questions.stem: Why would there be no trade winds or westerlies, only direct north-south winds, if Earth did not rotate?
options: The east-west deflection of moving air comes from Earth's rotation
Without rotation, the equator would no longer be heated more than the poles
Without rotation, air could not move from high to low pressure
The east-west winds are driven by the Moon's pull on the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Unequal heating would still drive air between the equator and the poles, but the Coriolis effect, which turns moving air east or west, exists only because Earth rotates. Rotation is also why the single equator-to-pole loop breaks into three cells in each hemisphere.

questions.stem: Why do the oceans act as a large heat sink in the Earth system?
options: Water has a high specific heat capacity, and the oceans are vast
Seawater has a high albedo, so it reflects most incoming heat
The oceans are heated mainly from below by Earth's interior
Salt in seawater absorbs heat and stores it as chemical energy
questions.explanation: Water needs a lot of energy to raise its temperature, and the oceans hold an enormous mass of it, so they absorb and store huge amounts of heat with only small temperature changes. Open ocean has a low albedo, so it absorbs most sunlight.

questions.stem: What drives the deep part of the global ocean conveyor?
options: Winds blowing across the ocean surface in the tropics
Heat rising from mid-ocean ridges on the sea floor
Differences in seawater density from temperature and salinity
Tides raised by the Moon's gravitational pull on the oceans
questions.explanation: Cold, salty water is dense and sinks, then spreads slowly along the ocean floor; this is why the deep conveyor is also called thermohaline circulation. Winds drive the surface currents, but the deep flow is density-driven.

questions.stem: Off the coast of Antarctica, sea ice forms each winter. How does this help to drive the ocean conveyor?
options: Salt left behind makes the cold water around it denser, so it sinks
The ice melts at once, warming the water so that it rises
Ice reflects sunlight, which pushes surface water towards the equator
Freezing removes water, so sea level falls and pulls water south
questions.explanation: When seawater freezes, most of the salt stays in the water, making it saltier. Cold, salty water is very dense, so it sinks to the ocean floor and spreads north as deep water. This sinking is one of the engines of the conveyor.

questions.stem: How does the global ocean conveyor affect the distribution of Earth's thermal energy?
options: It carries cold water from the poles to the surface at the equator only
It traps heat at the equator, making the tropics warmer than otherwise
It moves heat downward into Earth's crust beneath the sea floor
It carries warm surface water poleward and returns cold deep water
questions.explanation: Warm surface currents move heat from the tropics towards higher latitudes, where water cools, sinks and returns at depth. This transfer moderates the temperature difference between the equator and the poles. The heat stays in the ocean and atmosphere, not the crust.

questions.stem: Large amounts of fresh meltwater pour into the North Atlantic, where surface water normally sinks. What effect on the ocean conveyor would scientists expect?
options: It is unaffected, because only temperature controls seawater density
It slows, because fresher surface water is less dense and sinks less
It speeds up, because extra water adds weight that pushes deep water
It reverses, because fresh water always flows towards the equator
questions.explanation: Seawater density depends on both temperature and salinity. Fresh meltwater lowers the salinity, so the surface water is less dense and sinks less readily, weakening the conveyor. Temperature matters too, but it is not the only factor.

questions.stem: Earth's rotation affects the ocean as well as the air. How does it influence the large surface currents of the oceans?
options: It drags the deep ocean eastward faster than the surface water
It raises the sea floor near the equator, forcing currents poleward
It cools the western sides of oceans, making water sink there
It deflects wind-driven currents, turning them into large circular gyres
questions.explanation: Prevailing winds push surface water, and the Coriolis effect deflects the moving water, so surface currents form large loops called gyres, anticlockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. The East Australian Current is part of the South Pacific gyre.

questions.stem: In normal conditions over the tropical Pacific, which way do the trade winds blow and where does the warmest surface water collect?
options: North to south, piling warm water up near New Zealand and Antarctica
East to west, piling cold water up in the western Pacific near Indonesia
East to west, piling warm water up in the western Pacific near Indonesia
West to east, piling warm water up off the coast of South America
questions.explanation: The trade winds push warm surface water west, so a deep pool of warm water builds north of Australia. Off South America, cold, nutrient-rich water rises to replace it. This pattern is linked to the Walker circulation of rising air in the west and sinking air in the east.

questions.stem: During an El Niño event, what happens to the upwelling of cold water off the coast of Peru?
options: It strengthens, so surface water cools and fish catches increase
It stops completely and is replaced by downwelling of Antarctic ice
It moves to the western Pacific, cooling the seas off Indonesia
It weakens, so surface water warms and nutrient supply to fisheries falls
questions.explanation: With weaker trade winds, warm water spreads east and the cold upwelling off South America weakens. Less nutrient-rich water reaches the surface, so plankton and fish such as anchovies decline. Stronger upwelling and cooler water are features of La Niña.

questions.stem: Why does El Niño often bring drier conditions to eastern Australia?
options: The ozone layer thickens and blocks the energy needed for rain
The ocean conveyor stops, so no water evaporates near Australia
The warm water and rising air shift east, away from Australia
The trade winds strengthen and blow rain clouds away to the west
questions.explanation: In El Niño the warmest water and the rising, cloud-forming air move towards the central and eastern Pacific. Less moist air rises near Australia, so eastern Australia tends to get less rain, more heat and higher bushfire risk. The trade winds weaken, not strengthen.

questions.stem: Which conditions are typical of La Niña?
options: Weaker trade winds and warmer water off South America
Stronger trade winds and more rain over eastern Australia
Weaker trade winds and more rain over eastern Australia
Stronger trade winds and less rain over eastern Australia
questions.explanation: La Niña is an intensified version of the normal pattern: stronger trade winds push more warm water west, so more moist air rises near Australia, bringing above-average rain and flood risk to the east. Weaker trades and warmer water off South America describe El Niño.

questions.stem: Why are El Niño and La Niña described as anomalous weather patterns produced by atmosphere-ocean interaction?
options: They begin with earthquakes on the sea floor that move warm water
They are caused by the atmosphere alone, with no part played by the ocean
Changes in winds alter sea temperatures, which in turn alter the winds
They are caused by changes in the Sun's output that heat the oceans
questions.explanation: Weaker trade winds let warm water drift east; the warmer east then weakens the pressure difference that drives the trades, so they weaken further. This feedback between ocean and atmosphere shifts weather away from normal for months. Solar output and earthquakes are not the cause.

questions.stem: Data for a year show: trade winds stronger than normal, sea surface temperatures cooler than average in the eastern Pacific and warmer than average north of Australia. What should eastern Australian water managers prepare for?
options: An El Niño, with higher than average rainfall and flood risk
Neutral conditions, as these changes cancel each other out
A La Niña, with higher than average rainfall and flood risk
An El Niño, with lower than average rainfall and drought risk
questions.explanation: Stronger trades, cool water in the east and warm water in the west all point to La Niña, which typically brings wetter conditions and higher flood risk to eastern Australia. El Niño would show weak trades and warm water in the eastern Pacific.

questions.stem: How do El Niño and La Niña show that energy transfer between the ocean and atmosphere changes over time?
options: The location of warm water and rising air shifts, moving where heat is released
The total amount of solar energy reaching Earth doubles during each event
Heat from Earth's core is released into the Pacific during each event
The ocean stops absorbing solar energy until the event is over
questions.explanation: Warm ocean water heats the air above it and supplies moisture, and rising air releases that heat as clouds form. When the warm water shifts east or west, so does this heat release, changing circulation and rainfall far away. The Sun's input does not change.
